articles.title: Captain Smit Machchhar: The 'hero' India pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight
articles.summary: Capt Smit Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard the Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv.
articles.body:
The pilot who was stabbed on an Israel-bound flight on Wednesday has been identified as Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar.

Capt Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, forcing the plane to divert to Saudi Arabia.

The captain, who has been hailed as a "true hero" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, was taken to a hospital in Tabuk, a city in north-western Saudi Arabia, where he remains in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Riyadh.

Writing on X, Netanyahu said Capt Machchhar "saved the lives of 174 people" and prevented "a catastrophic mid-air disaster".

Capt Machchhar grew up in the Indian city of Mumbai, where his parents still live. In 2008, he joined Mainland Air, an aviation college in New Zealand's Dunedin, before joining Indian airline SpiceJet as a commercial pilot three years later. He moved to Dubai and joined Flydubai in 2022, having become an experienced pilot.

Speaking to the BBC, Philip Kean, the CEO of Mainland Air, said he remembers Capt Machchhar as a man who would remain calm in a crisis.

"We trained him for forced landing - not this kind of situation, which is very, very rare," Kean said. "It was a long time back but he came across as a good and honest worker."

Capt Machchhar has more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile.

His former employer SpiceJet issued a statement calling Machchhar a "hero" who had saved "countless lives".

Last year, Capt Machchhar spoke about how he started flying and his experiences as a pilot on a podcast called Bona-Fide Banter.

Aviation, he said, was "never a childhood dream". When he was around 19, he joined a management course, planning to work with his family's business. But then he came across an aviation seminar and "the bug bit [him]," he added.

Machchhar also spoke about how, when he wore his pilot's uniform, he was "no-nonsense" and thought "about work 100%". But unlike his younger days, he added, he now placed a greater value on having a healthy work-life balance and spending time with family.

"Give personal life equal importance - it will help you fly longer," he advised.

He also detailed challenges he had faced in the air, including when a passenger went into early labour and the crew worked together to ensure the baby was born safely.

"In aviation terms, I was lucky to grow up with people who helped me be the pilot that I am today," he said, crediting senior pilots with teaching him how to face stressful situations.

At the time of the conversation, Capt Machchhar said that no plane he'd flown had had to make an emergency landing. He had, however, faced medical emergencies and minor aircraft issues causing delays.

He said delays were "not my problem. As long as you're walking out of the aircraft [safely], that's what I want."

Indian social media has been awash with praise for Capt Machchhar since his identity emerged, with commenters calling him a hero. Snippets from the podcast have also gone viral.

What we know about stabbing on Flydubai flight to Israel

Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the United Arab Emirates at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time) en route to Ben Gurion Airport in Israel.

The flight was carrying at least 150 people, with Netanyahu saying "almost all" passengers were Israeli.

Data from flight tracking website Flightradar24 shows the plane made a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia around two and a half hours after take-off, dropping more than 17,000ft (5,000m) in less than two minutes at around 05:21.

Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code, which indicates a hijacking.

At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.

Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.

Initial local media reports cited Israeli officials as saying a fight had broken out between two pilots.

But speaking on Wednesday after the incident, Netanyahu confirmed later reports that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane.

He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member broke into the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".

The plane was diverted to Tabuk Airport in north-western Saudi Arabia and touched down at 06:58, according to location data.

The stabbed pilot, who is in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia, was later identified as Capt Machchhar.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Machchhar "showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others" despite being seriously injured.

"His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy," he wrote in a post on X, adding that he hoped for the pilot's speedy recovery.

Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar praised the pilot's "extraordinary courage and remarkable presence of mind, even in the face of grave danger".

Speaking to reporters at the White House, US President Donald Trump said that "the pilot was in very bad shape" but had the sense to open the cockpit door during the attack.

"Amazing, in a way he was a hero, to open the door. He was able to fall back and get the door open."

Too early to say what motive for Dubai-Tel Aviv flight attack was, Israeli PM says

articles.title: Wicknell Chivayo: Zimbabwean businessman and wife killed in helicopter crash
articles.summary: Chivayo was known for his lavish lifestyle, close ties to African presidents and lucrative government contracts.
articles.body:
Prominent Zimbabwean businessman Wicknell Chivayo and his wife have been killed in a helicopter crash that left six people dead, his family have confirmed.

The helicopter came down in the Marondera rural area, about 70km (43 miles) east of the capital, Harare, on Wednesday evening. Police said all six people on board died.

Family spokesperson Herbert Chivayo confirmed the deaths of the 43-year-old businessman and his wife Lucy Muteke to state broadcaster ZBC, saying the family was devastated by the tragedy.

Chivayo was known for his lavish lifestyle, close ties to some African presidents and lucrative government contracts that had repeatedly attracted scrutiny.

He had denied allegations of wrongdoing linked to his business dealings.

Police spokesperson Commissioner Paul Nyathi said the aircraft crashed at about 17:00 local time (15:00 GMT) and had six occupants, but authorities did not immediately identify all those on board. Two of the six were pilots, according to government officials.

ZBC reported that the group was travelling from Gandami in Chikomba, where Chivayo and his wife were building a rural home, when the helicopter crashed at Kudenga Farm about 40 minutes after take-off.

"We are at a loss for words after the tragic news," the family spokesperson, told the ZBC.

The cause of the crash was not immediately known, and police said investigations were under way. Emergency services were sent to the scene on Wednesday evening.

How a self-styled knight giving away cars and wads of cash got people talking

Earlier, government spokesman Nick Mangwana confirmed the crash, saying the helicopter was carrying "a prominent businessman, three other passengers and two pilots".

"Current information indicates that there were no survivors in this crash," Mangwana posted on X.

On Thursday, aviation officials led by Transport Minister Felix Mhona arrived at the crash site, where investigators recovered the aircraft's intact black box as they began investigating.

"Preliminary findings show that fuel spilled on impact, followed by a fire that burnt the grass at the crash site," said George Mashababe, director general of the Civil Aviation Authority of Zimbabwe.

"The cause of the crash is yet to be ascertained."

Despite serving several years in prison after being convicted of fraud in 2004, Chivayo went on to build a successful business career, mostly through government contracts.

He was the managing director of Intratrek Zimbabwe and had built a high public profile through his philanthropy and displays of wealth on social media.

Among his best-known business ventures was a $172m (£128m) solar power project in Gwanda awarded to Intratrek by the state-owned Zimbabwe Power Company. The project became the subject of years of legal disputes.

He also came under scrutiny over the procurement of materials for Zimbabwe's disputed 2023 elections. Zimbabwe's anti-corruption commission investigated allegations surrounding contracts awarded to South African company Ren-Form but closed the inquiry in 2025, saying it had found no evidence linking Chivayo or the Zimbabwe Electoral Commission to wrongdoing.

Widely known as "Sir Wicknell", Chivayo frequently used the title publicly and on social media, although he was never given a British knighthood.

He was also known for giving away luxury cars and large sums of money to musicians, religious leaders and other public figures, often publicising the gifts on social media.

In a statement, President Emmerson Mnangagwa said he had met Chivayo after a cabinet meeting just a day before his death, when the businessman shared some of his plans for Zimbabwe.

"We are all shattered by this unexpected, sudden demise of so young a family," Mnangagwa said, describing Chivayo as "consummately philanthropic", saying his family had "touched so many lives" through their acts of charity and generosity.

Mnangagwa said Chivayo's death had left him "personally numbed" and in "great shock".

His connections extended beyond Zimbabwe.

Kenya's President William Ruto, who had previously appeared in public with Chivayo, paid tribute to him as a "dear friend" and sent condolences to the families of those killed.

"I will remember him for his friendship, his energy and his deep conviction in the possibilities of our continent," Ruto added.

Kenyan opposition figures had questioned Chivayo's repeated access to Ruto and State House.

He frequently publicised his access to African leaders, posting photographs of meetings with presidents including Zambia's Hakainde Hichilema, South Africa's Cyril Ramaphosa and Tanzania's Samia Suluhu Hassan, as well as Eswatini's King Mswati III.

articles.title: Dame Esther Rantzen: Tributes paid to 'inspirational' presenter and Childline founder
articles.summary: Dame Esther Rantzen was "an inspirational individual", the director of her Childline helpline says.
articles.body:
Dame Esther Rantzen was "an inspirational individual" who was "quite a force" as a campaigner, according to the director of Childline, the children's helpline founded by the broadcaster in the 1980s.

"She inspired people, she energised people, she persuaded people," Shaun Friel told BBC Breakfast. "She had a great mind and she had obviously that natural journalistic ability."

Dame Esther, who died on Wednesday at the age of 86, was known for presenting BBC consumer show That's Life! for 21 years, and for campaigning on issues including child welfare and assisted dying.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham led the tributes, saying the veteran broadcaster had "changed countless lives".

BBC director general Matt Brittin also paid tribute to Dame Esther, describing her as a "legend of British broadcasting" whose contribution to public life was "immeasurable".

"Her warmth, spirit and fight for justice and action that we saw on our screens continued long after the programme ended, with a lifetime of campaigning where she changed the lives of millions," he said.

Fellow broadcaster and money saving expert Martin Lewis called Dame Esther an "inspiration" and a "pioneer" whose "impact and memory will long continue to shine".

Chris Sherwood, chief executive of the NSPCC, which runs Childline, said Dame Esther had gone to "exceptional lengths to ensure children and young people across the UK had somewhere to turn when they were in need of help".

Dame Esther set up the telephone helpline in 1986 after featuring a number of incidents of child abuse and neglect on That's Life! and realising that many children had nowhere to turn.

How That's Life! gave Esther Rantzen a career-defining moment

Dame Esther Rantzen: That's Life! presenter, Childline founder and campaigner for assisted dying

Veteran broadcaster Dame Esther Rantzen dies aged 86

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Friel said: "The legacy that Dame Esther created when she created Childline is something quite incredible. She changed how society looked upon children."

He added: "When she decided she had a vision or something had to be done or had to be changed, she was quite a force."

TV executive Michael Grade paid tribute to "her courage and her fortitude and what she achieved in her life".

Lord Grade told BBC Radio 4's Today: "She used her television fame to help an awful lot of people, particularly the children. And Childline goes on today, getting so many calls from distressed and abused children.

"That was an extraordinary effort of will to turn the television programme into a long-lasting charity that's so effective and so needed. That's her legacy for me. I'll always remember her for that."

Childline merged with the NSPCC in 2006. In 2013, Dame Esther founded The Silver Line to help older people suffering from isolation and loneliness.

She also led campaigns on car safety, organ donation and bullying, and later in life became a prominent campaigner for the legalisation of assisted dying.

She had been terminally ill with lung cancer. In 2023, she revealed she had joined Dignitas, the Swiss assisted dying clinic, but last month said she was now "too physically fragile to make the journey".

Burnham said he would "always admire the characteristic courage and openness with which she spoke about her illness, making us all think about the difficult questions we face at the end of life".

Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who sponsored the assisted dying bill, told the BBC that Dame Esther was a "wonderful mix of strength and feistiness, but also really deep compassion and kindness" - and that she would continue to inspire campaigners.

Baroness Jan Royall, former leader of the House of Lords and a friend of Dame Esther, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Thursday that she was a "formidable" person.

"She was an extraordinary, compassionate woman, a passionate woman, and she brought about such change in our world, change for the better."

Baroness Royall added that Dame Esther had "a wicked sense of humour" and a "zest for life", which was the thing that "drove her to try and improve people's lives through Silver Line, Childline etc, but also with the assisted dying bill."

Broadcaster Gyles Brandreth told Radio 4's Today: "I was lucky enough to know her for more than 50 years, and what I remember is her energy, her intelligence, her resilience. Her vulgar streak, which she enjoyed and she said she got from her mother. She was formidable and she was fun."

Dame Esther told him her campaigning was rooted in memories of difficult times in her own life as a child during and after World War Two, Brandreth said.

Dame Esther's That's Life! co-presenter Bill Buckley told the BBC's Radio 4 Front Row programme that "nothing would stop her" when it came to campaigning.

"She saw the light at the end of the tunnel and followed it doggedly," he said.

Dame Elaine Paige, known for her roles in West End productions like Cats and Evita, paid tribute to a "great broadcaster, journalist and campaigner".

She said: "Her Childline, the confidential counselling service for young people in distress, helped so many children and The Silver Line was aimed at older people suffering loneliness and isolation."

Anton Du Beke, Dame Esther's partner on Strictly Come Dancing, shared a photo of the pair dancing together in the 2004 series, writing that the two had "remained firm friends" ever since.

He praised her "breadth of knowledge and passion" and called her "the ultimate breaker of the glass ceiling", adding: "She will be greatly missed and my sincere thoughts are with her family."

Davina McCall wrote on Instagram that Dame Esther had "made the world a better place, and inspired so many of us to do better and live life to its fullest."

The message accompanied a video of the former Big Brother host discussing how Dame Esther was an "inspiration to girls like me when we were growing up".

Presenter Amol Rajan said Dame Esther "changed the course of millions of lives" as he paid tribute, calling her "an inspirational, strong woman ahead of her time".

"Not bad for a bright, Hertfordshire girl born during the early stages of the Second World War."

Watch BBC media editor Katie Razzall's half-hour special programme Esther! on iPlayer . It will also be shown this Friday, 2 October, on BBC One at 19:30 BST.

articles.title: A Gutenberg Bible leaf bought for £25 in the early 20th century was rediscovered among a grandfather's belongings in an English attic; the roughly 570-year-old page fetched £39,000 at auction in 2025
articles.summary: A single page from one of the most important books in printing history spent decades sitting unnoticed in an English attic.
articles.body: A single page from one of the most important books in printing history spent decades sitting unnoticed in an English attic. Bought for just £25 in the early 20th century, the roughly 570-year-old leaf from the Gutenberg Bible was rediscovered among a grandfather’s belongings and eventually sold at auction for £39,000 in 2025.The rare page was found by a resident of Bromsgrove, Worcestershire, among possessions belonging to his late grandfather. The items had been stored in a box in the family attic that had remained unopened for more than 50 years. The family reportedly believed the Bible leaf had originally belonged to the man's great-grandfather, an early 20th-century traveller and collector who visited Europe and the Far East and was known to frequent auction rooms.The family had first seen the collection around 2000, after the man's grandmother died, but it was only in 2024 that they decided to have the items examined and authenticated. When the box eventually reached Chorley’s Auctioneers, the significance of one particular sheet became clear.What appeared to be an old page was in fact a leaf from the Gutenberg Bible, printed in Mainz, Germany, around 1455 by Johannes Gutenberg and Johann Fust.From £25 purchase to £39,000 auction saleThe page was offered as Lot 401 at Chorley’s March 2025 auction in the Cotswolds. Before the sale, it carried an estimate of £20,000 to £30,000. It ultimately exceeded that estimate, selling for £39,000 at the March 25 auction. Antiques Trade Gazette reported that the £39,000 figure was the hammer price, before the buyer’s premium.The original £25 purchase is part of the object's remarkable story. The surviving documentation indicates that the leaf may have been among the individual Gutenberg Bible leaves sold by American antiquarian bookseller Gabriel Wells in the 1920s.Chorley’s catalogue notes that the leaf came with loose pages from A. Edward Newton’s 1921 essay 'A Noble Fragment', which accompanied Gutenberg Bible leaves distributed by Wells. The auction house cautioned that this material does not conclusively prove the leaf was one of Wells’ original sales, but said it lends credibility to that possible provenance.Wells had acquired an incomplete Gutenberg Bible and made the controversial decision to dismantle it, selling individual leaves to collectors. According to Chorley’s, leaves in good condition were selling for an average of about $150 at the time, while damaged examples were priced around $100.What was once considered an acceptable way of distributing pieces of a damaged historic book is viewed very differently today.What is on the 570-year-old page?The leaf measures approximately 39.2 by 28.6 centimetres and contains 42 lines of text arranged in two columns. It comes from the Book of Numbers, covering parts of verses 8:13 through 10:23. The passages include the setting apart of the Levites, the Passover and the account of the cloud above the Tabernacle.Despite being more than five centuries old, the page retains striking details. The text is printed in Gothic type, while the initials were added in red and blue. The chapter heading letters also alternate between the two colours.The auction house described the leaf as an incunabulum, a term used for books printed in Europe during the earliest period of printing with movable type, generally before 1501.The page was not flawless. Its condition report noted toning and foxing, a central fold with some wear, marginal browning and chipping, and slight loss to one upper corner. There was also some staining from the page-edge colouring and evidence of an inked number on the inner margin. Yet its historical importance far outweighed those imperfections.The book that changed printingThe Gutenberg Bible is widely regarded as the first substantial book printed with movable type in the Western world. Its production in Mainz in the mid-15th century by Johannes Gutenberg marked a major turning point in the history of European printing.Before the spread of movable-type printing, books had to be copied by hand, a painstaking process that made them expensive and limited their availability. Gutenberg’s printing methods allowed multiple copies of a large book to be produced with far greater efficiency.The Gutenberg Bible was printed in an edition of roughly 180 copies on paper and vellum. Chorley’s says the original edition contained more than 640 leaves and would have taken several years and a team of workers to produce.Only 49 complete copies or substantial portions are currently known to have survived, according to the auction house. No complete Gutenberg Bible has been sold at auction since 1978, making individual leaves an important way for collectors and institutions to acquire a physical fragment of the historic work.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2023, British rail researchers tested crushed old glass in place of scarce rail sand; it gave trains comparable grip and caused similar rail wear in wet and leaf-covered tests
articles.summary: In 2023, British researchers explore the feasibility of using crushed recycled glass instead of traditional rail sand to improve train grip during wet and leaf-covered conditions, revealing promising results.
articles.body: Each autumn, railway workers in Britain get ready for the same slippery situation. Leaves fall on to the track, are mashed by the wheels and turn into a slippery film that is notoriously difficult for trains to get a grip on. The long-standing remedy has been to blow a little sand on to the rail just in front of the wheels. The trouble is that sand is not as plentiful as it once seemed, so a group of British researchers has been testing whether crushed recycled glass could take its place.It’s worth a moment on the broader backdrop. Sand is used in concrete, asphalt and glass and the UN Environment Programme has estimated that the global use of sand and gravel is around 50 billion tonnes a year, making it the second most used resource on earth after water. Rail sanding uses a small amount of it, but when a material is being stretched in all directions, even small users have good reason to seek a substitute.How rail sanding worksAt the tiny contact area between a steel wheel and a steel rail, friction allows trains to accelerate and decelerate. Engineers call it low adhesion when water, oil or a coating of crushed leaves destroys that hold. Spraying grains onto the rail in front of the wheel solves the issue. This is known as sanding. As the wheel rolls over the grains, they split and spread out, packing them into clusters of fine powder. This grinding action raises the friction back to a manageable level. Sand is automatically shot on certain British passenger trains when wheel slip is detected during more forceful braking, and it always descends when the emergency brake is applied.It works, but it generates a lot of waste. The analysis of the field records shows that more than 80 per cent of the sprayed sand can be lost, because so little of it really penetrates the contact. This makes a substitution attractive, and glass is an obvious alternative. Glass is made largely of silica, the main component of natural sand, and there is plenty of waste glass to spare. One academic analysis puts worldwide glass trash in 2018 at roughly 130 million tonnes, of which only around 21 per cent was recycled. The underlying challenge was whether crushed glass could hold onto a slick rail as well as sand does, and that required correct measuring.Glass testingSadaf Maramizonouz and colleagues at Newcastle University and the University of Sheffield published two related papers in 2023. A dataset in Scientific Data characterised seven candidate materials, including standard Great British rail sand, Austrian rail sand, waste glass beads, recycled crushed glass, two types of alumina and dolomite. A separate study in the Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Journal of Rail and Rapid Transit, examined the recycled crushed glass in detail. The researchers measured density, grain size, shape and how the grains behave in bulk, since a grain's strength and shape matter as much as its chemistry.Then came the tests. Using a high-pressure torsion rig, a laboratory device that mimics the squeeze between wheel and rail, the researchers compared recycled glass with standard sand in dry, wet and leaf-contaminated conditions. The wet and leafy runs are the low-adhesion conditions that cause the most trouble for railways.What the findings tell usThe main finding is reassuring. Recycled glass provided an acceptable level of traction and caused a similar level of rail damage to standard rail sand, according to the study in the Proceedings of the IMechE. The wear result matters as much as the grip: sanding already wears wheels and rails, so an alternative that gripped well but ate through steel faster would only shift the cost elsewhere.Some caution is necessary, however. This was lab research, and real track brings in variables no rig can properly replicate. Other research shows that the way grains spread on the rail differs between dry and wet conditions; thus, glass would need testing on a live track, including checks on cost and on the reliability of the supply of clean crushed glass in bulk. For now the message is simple: in damp, leafy lab conditions, crushed old bottles gave grip and rail wear comparable to sand. Railways will still need real-world trials before glass replaces sand in the sanders, but the idea has passed an important test.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Kentucky woman started a $300 eBay side hustle in 2011, left her $35,000 insurance job in 2014; 10 years later, Pink Lily reached $141 million
articles.summary: In 2011, Tori and Chris Gerbig were not setting out to build a large fashion retailer.
articles.body: In 2011, Tori and Chris Gerbig were not setting out to build a large fashion retailer. They were a young Kentucky couple with an interest in affordable women’s clothing and about $300 to put into a small online venture. Writing for CNBC in 2022, Tori revealed that she was still working in insurance, at that time while the clothing business ran alongside their jobs and family life. What began with listings on eBay gradually developed into Pink Lily, an online fashion company based in Bowling Green, Kentucky. Ten years after that first investment, the business reported $141 million in gross sales for the year, illustrating how a modest online shop had grown into a sizeable retail operation.How a $300 eBay clothing side hustle became Pink LilyThe Gerbigs launched their eBay shop in 2011 after noticing that finding fashionable women's clothes at relatively low prices was not always straightforward. They put roughly $300 into their first batch of clothing and accessories, buying stock through a wholesale website.At that stage, the operation was deliberately small. Tori continued working her insurance job while she and Chris handled orders from their living room. There was little in the way of fixed business overhead, although shipping costs had to be covered.Their approach to pricing was fairly simple at first. Tori had no previous experience in retail pricing, so she based prices on what she would have been willing to pay as a customer. The business was not producing anything close to the figures it would later report, but it was generating enough to keep the experiment going.During the first few years, monthly profits generally ranged between $300 and $1,000. Rather than treating that money as household income, the couple used it to pay down student loans and buy more stock.How Tori Gerbig took Pink Lily from eBay to its own websiteThe business began to take on a different shape as Tori spent more time building relationships with suppliers. She travelled to Los Angeles to meet vendors and began attending trade shows, giving the couple access to a wider selection of products.In 2013, Tori also created a Facebook group to promote the clothing to potential customers. The group helped create a direct line between the business and shoppers, particularly around Bowling Green, Kentucky.That year proved important for the company. The Gerbigs had accumulated about $20,000 from the business, which they used to build an official website for Pink Lily. The move took the operation beyond its original eBay model and gave the couple a dedicated place to sell their growing range. The change was followed by a sharp increase in revenue.Tori and Chris Gerbig take Pink Lily full-time as sales surgeBy May 2014, Pink Lily was generating more than $100,000 in monthly revenue. After three years of running the business alongside her employment, Tori left her insurance sales job of earning $35,000 per year and began working on Pink Lily full-time.Chris followed several months later. His role centred on the company's finances and operations, while the business continued expanding its product range and customer base. Pink Lily finished 2014 with more than $4 million in revenue. The figures were a long way from the $300 monthly investment that had started the venture just a few years earlier.The company continued to grow over the following years. By 2019, Pink Lily had recorded $70 million in total sales and brought in a minority investment to help support its expansion.From an eBay shop to a larger retail operationBy the time Gerbig described the company's progress in 2022, Pink Lily was selling more than 11,000 products on its website and had also opened a physical shop. The business employed about 250 full-time workers in Bowling Green, where it had become one of the larger employers in the area.The Gerbigs still attended trade shows, but Pink Lily had developed a core group of vendor relationships and was working with partners on custom designs. That represented a considerable shift from the couple's original model of buying clothing wholesale and listing individual items on eBay. The company had developed its own retail identity and a much larger supply operation.Then came the sales figure that put the scale of that expansion into perspective. In 2021, Pink Lily generated $141 million in gross sales, according to Gerbig's account published by CNBC in February 2022.Social media became part of the retail modelPink Lily's growth was also tied to how the company used social media. Rather than treating platforms such as Instagram simply as advertising channels, the business used its audience to gather feedback about products and potential brands. Customers were asked what they wanted to see on the website and in the shop. The company could then use those responses when deciding which products to stock.The strategy extended to customers sharing photographs of their purchases. Pink Lily sent orders in branded bags and encouraged shoppers to post their outfits using the company's hashtag. Some of that customer content was then featured on the Pink Lily website.Tori Gerbig said, “At first, it was just a fun hobby. Little did I know, 10 years later, my husband Chris and I would be running Pink Lily full-time. Last year, our online clothing business generated $141 million in gross sales. And today, our social media audience has grown to 3.6 million followers.”Customers were also used as brand ambassadorsPink Lily developed a paid ambassador programme around some of its longstanding customers. Participants received a 10% commission on sales generated through their promotion of the brand. It was not a small part of the company's marketing activity. Gerbig said the ambassador programme generated about $7.5 million in sales in 2021.The model gave Pink Lily another way of reaching shoppers through people who already bought its products. Instead of relying entirely on conventional advertising, the company incorporated existing customers into its sales and promotional system.Pink Lily bought entire inventories to offer exclusive clothingAs Pink Lily became larger, the Gerbigs also looked for ways to make some of its merchandise less interchangeable with products available from other retailers. In certain cases, the company would purchase a vendor's entire inventory of a particular item. That meant the same product could not simply appear elsewhere through another retailer using the same supplier. This approach helped Pink Lily assemble collections that were specific to its own store rather than relying exclusively on products that shoppers could find across multiple online retailers.What started in a living room had become a $141 million businessThe distance between Pink Lily's first year and its reported 2021 sales is substantial. The company began with about $300 worth of inventory, a living-room workspace and two people managing the operation around existing commitments. Three years later, Tori had left her insurance career after the side business began generating six-figure monthly revenue. Chris then joined her full-time, and the company moved from a small eBay seller into its own online retail operation.By 2021, Pink Lily had reached $141 million in gross sales, employed around 250 people and sold thousands of products through its website and physical shop. The business had also taken outside minority investment and developed a network of suppliers and customer ambassadors.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Ball State buried about 3,600 geothermal wells beneath its Indiana campus; the system now heats and cools 47 buildings and saves roughly $2 million a year
articles.summary: Ball State University transforms its energy system by installing the largest geothermal heating and cooling network in the US, saving approximately $2 million annually and significantly reducing carbon emissions.
articles.body: For nearly 70 years, Ball State University in Muncie, Indiana, relied on coal to heat its campus during winter. The campus heating plant had four coal-fired boilers that burned, according to later estimates, about 36,000 tons of coal a year to keep classrooms and residence halls warm. But as the equipment aged and the cost of installing a new fossil fuel boiler increased, university leaders began to look at renewable options instead. The university has installed a campus-wide geothermal network that now supplies heating and cooling across much of the campus.According to the US Department of Energy, it is one of the country’s largest ground-source geothermal heating and cooling systems. Construction began in 2009 to replace four coal-fired boilers and eventually provide heating and cooling to 47 buildings across the campus. Geothermal heat pumps had long been used to heat and cool individual buildings, but applying the technology at this campus scale was unprecedented at the time.Why did the university digCoal was turning into a bad investment. The boilers were getting older and less dependable, and the cost of a new fossil fuel unit would have increased with each passing year. The university decided to transform the entire campus after a proof of concept trial persuaded the team that a ground source heat pump system could supply both hot and chilled water.Not everyone saw that as wise. Two reputable geothermal system designers informed project manager Jim Lowe they weren't sure a system this big would be practical and effective, according to Ball State's own magazine. Drilling started in July 2009 after Lowe refused to accept that. The remaining coal-fired boilers were shut down in March 2014. The bill arrived at $83 million, covered by state appropriations and federal grants, including Recovery Act money.How the ground does the workA few feet below the surface, the ground remains close to 55 degrees Fahrenheit, providing a relatively stable temperature that engineers can use as a source of heat in winter and a place to reject heat in summer. About 3,600 boreholes, each roughly 400 feet deep, were drilled across campus, and every one holds a loop of pipe sealed in grout. Because this is a closed-loop system, fresh water circulates through the pipes without ever touching natural groundwater.In winter, heat pumps extract heat from that fluid and transfer it into the buildings. In summer, the process reverses: heat is extracted from the buildings and released back into the ground. There are two district energy stations, one north and one south, with four heat pump chillers, each of 2,500 tonnes. About 10 miles of distribution piping connect the energy stations to campus buildings, while the borehole fields contain roughly 1,000 miles of smaller geothermal piping.How the system worksThe system has also substantially reduced the university's carbon footprint by replacing coal-fired heating. The campus is avoiding the burning of coal, thus saving roughly 85,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, along with reductions in sulphur dioxide, particulate matter and coal ash, the engineers’ design summary said.It's not all one-sided. Ball State's project analysis found that the geothermal system could reduce overall energy use and carbon dioxide emissions compared with continuing to rely on the coal-fired boilers. The project also required a substantial upfront investment, making state and federal support important to its development.But the initiative has attracted interest far beyond Indiana. Ball State said tour groups from Germany, Iceland, Japan and South Korea had visited the two energy stations. One of the project engineers later worked on a geothermal system at Ford Motor Co.'s world headquarters.The lesson is practical for colleges and towns facing the same issue. A complete loop of wells can replace coal for heating and cooling at the district level and can pay off in lower running costs and healthier air, if there is money to cover the drilling. Ball State was among the first universities to use a geothermal system at this scale, and the boreholes beneath the campus now perform much of the heating and cooling work once supplied by coal.You use AI every day. articles.title: Chita Andolan is back: Why are Madhya Pradesh's Panna villagers protesting against Ken-Betwa project
articles.summary: Remember the unnerving visuals from Chita Andolan in Madhya Pradesh? Displaced Tribals sleeping on pyres, standing in water for their compensation.
articles.body: Remember the unnerving visuals from Chita Andolan in Madhya Pradesh? Displaced Tribals sleeping on pyres, standing in water for their compensation. The unique protest is back and in its 20th day with agitators battling rain, waterlogging, lathicharge and general apathy by the authorities.Activist Amit Bhatnagar, Jai Kisan Sangathan leader, who has been on a hunger strike for the past four days, was arrested on Wednesday as protesters demonstrated chita, jal, sooli, mitti, bhook (pyre, water, gallows, soil, hunger) other forms of satyagraha.What is happening in Madhya Pradesh's Panna?Bhatnagar accused the Panna administration of suppressing the agitation by lathicharging protesters, including women.Speaking to TOI before his arrest, Bhatnagar said, "For the past three days, the police have been bringing along people dressed in plain clothes, who misbehaved with women, entered their homes and even took away people’s phones which have still not been returned. When we approach the police, they ask who took the phones. How are people supposed to identify every face and find out who took them?""There is an atmosphere of fear in the villages. If we say anything, they start resorting to lathi-charge and filing false cases against the protesters," he added. “I am courting arrest because democracy is being murdered. Are we not even allowed to protest peacefully? We are putting ourselves through hardship to raise our concerns, but instead of listening to us, they have cut off the electricity and water. Even the British never did this.”So why are the protesters back?The latest protest follows a 15-day agitation in July, led largely by tribal women, after which the administration had assured protesters that eligible and genuinely displaced families would be transparently included in compensation and rehabilitation lists.However, the protesters claimed that they did not get the promised compensation. Also, their houses were now inundated, with two to three feet of water entering homes in several villages which now stand waterlogged including Mandalia, Tapariya and Kuwarpur."The families whose houses have been submerged are so poor that they have been forced to continue living there, or put up one makeshift shelter next to another, and then another. Earlier, the water would rise by half a foot at a time. But this time there was heavy rain on the 26th and 27th of September, followed by a 24-hour red alert, leaving them with no time to move. The villages turned into islands,” said Bhatnagar.The protesters claim that the compensation process remains incomplete, with several families receiving only Rs 5 lakh despite the government announcing a Rs 12.5-lakh package.They are also opposing the compensation conditions, which makes several tribals ineligible for relief.“The cut-off date under Section 11 has been set as 2018, which means people who are now 25-26 years old have received nothing. Those who are older are getting only Rs 5 lakh. What are families with eight or 10 children supposed to do?" asked Bhatnagar, adding that they were not against development projects, but that this development should not come at the cost of the rights of tribals.Bhatnagar pointed to Section 38 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, which he said raised concerns about any displacement or submergence taking place before compensation and rehabilitation obligations had been fulfilled.“Villages and homes are now submerged. Houses have started collapsing and water has entered them. Yet, Section 38 of the 2013 law says that compensation for an irrigation project should be paid six months before submergence. If the houses were submerged two months ago, compensation should have been paid eight months earlier,” he said.The authorities, on the other hand, claim that they have been conducting fresh surveys and distributing compensation to affected families. TOI reached out to Chhatarpur district magistrate and is still awaiting a response from the administration.What is the project aiming to accomplish?The Majhgawan dam project aims to transfer surplus water from Ken river to Betwa through the Daudhan Dam, a network of tunnels and a 221-km canal. It is supposed to address water shortages in drought-prone Bundelkhand region that spans across Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.The project traces back to a plan introduced in 1980 and cleared in 2021 to connect the rivers. Prime Minister Narendra Modi laid its foundation stone in December 2024.The project is expected to improve agricultural output, curb migration and strengthen groundwater recharge through the revival of traditional Chandela-era ponds.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: I escaped communism. America must not ignore the urgent warning signs
articles.summary: The record is unambiguous and is written in blood. No communist revolution has delivered the justice, equality and prosperity it promised.
articles.body: I am an immigrant from Colombia, a country that the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) — a communist revolutionary group — spent half a century tearing apart. FARC murdered thousands of Colombians through sanctioned massacres, kidnappings, and terrorism, and the war the FARC drove displaced over 7 million Colombians, resulting in one of the largest internal displacement crises in the world. I am now a naturalized citizen of the United States, a country that millions from around the world are still trying to reach. So, I read the latest polling on American capitalism with a particular kind of alarm. This polling is the result of a survey released by The Free Press using a method to surface the opinions people keep to themselves. The finding: just one in three Americans holds a positive view of capitalism. Not one in three Democrats. One in three Americans. Before the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) take a victory lap, consider the rest. That same survey found that most Americans remain wary of socialism, and Gallup found that while capitalism drew 54% approval, free enterprise drew 81% and small business 95%, compared with 37% for big business. Americans have not turned against free enterprise, ownership or entrepreneurial risk. Yet DSA candidates keep winning elections. The gap between Americans’ faith in free enterprise and the DSA’s wins is a real vulnerability, and it deserves an honest question: Why not communism? MORE AMERICANS THAN EVER NOW HAVE A POSITIVE VIEW OF SOCIALISM, NEW POLL SAYS An honest answer requires an important clarification. There is no meaningful difference between socialism and communism, and the founders of the movement said so without pretense. Lenin devoted chapters of "The State and Revolution" to expounding on Marx and what he called the first phase of communist society and its ultimate end. Socialism was never the alternative to communism. It was the on-ramp. There is no meaningful difference between socialism and communism, and the founders of the movement said so without pretense. Socialism was never the alternative to communism. It was the on-ramp. So why not take it? Because the record is unambiguous and is written in blood. No communist revolution has delivered the justice, equality, and prosperity it promised. Estimates place the death toll of communist regimes near 100 million across Russia, Eastern Europe, China, Africa and South America. And consider one plain fact. No communist state in history has been concerned about people sneaking in. Every one of them has had to worry about people getting out, a concern that produced a heavily guarded 4,300-mile Iron Curtain across Europe built to face inward. Nations that people flee have not solved anything. SOCIALISM WILL 'CONTROL PEOPLE' AND 'TAKE EVERYTHING AWAY' FROM AMERICA, ACCORDING TO THESE EXPATS Yet the communist appeal is real, and pretending otherwise is foolish. Communism begins by naming a genuine pain. American capitalism is too much big-business economics with its ethos of the very large, the consolidated, and the impersonal. This makes the household, the small business and the ordinary person willing to take a risk weaker and less important. Millions of Americans experience this as a shrinking future and a loss of control over their destiny. The communist arrives, agrees with them and offers the oldest bargain on record: "You have nothing to lose but your chains. Workers of the world, unite!" Communism is the opium Marx accused religion of being, and it has never once healed the pain. It has not expanded economic freedom; it has abolished it through central planning. Communism did not restore personal agency; it destroyed agency on principle because agency is precisely what a total state cannot permit. MODERN CAPITALISM IS TURNING 250, TOO. WE NEED TO REMIND AMERICANS WHY IT’S IMPORTANT All imposters have an element of truth, and communism is no different. What the communist gets right but then betrays is the truth that the core of economics is the human person. But the communist cannot say why. If we are only producers and consumers, then personal agency is a mere preference, not a fundamental part of our humanity, and the state may override it whenever it deems it expedient to do so. Communism is the opium Marx accused religion of being, and it has never once healed the pain. It has not expanded economic freedom. It has abolished it through central planning. The truth about the human person that no materialism — capitalist or communist — can say is what the Christian account of the human person defends: human beings bear the image of God. Work is therefore noble rather than a mere function. Ownership is a stewardship, not evidence of superiority. And human dignity is not for the state to grant or revoke. The dignity of the human person is divinely endowed and is protected and nurtured through economic freedom and personal agency. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The time is short, and I write to my fellow Americans as someone who has seen where this road ends. Let’s not take the bargain the communists offer. Let’s get out of our echo chambers and get to know each other again. Let’s elect leaders who will expand economic freedom rather than administer its disappearance. And to my fellow college and university presidents: our campuses should be places where these arguments are discussed honestly, thoughtfully and in public, with no quarter given to censorship, to violence against those with whom we disagree or to indoctrination hiding behind academic freedom. articles.title: Ivan Toney denies Soho nightclub assault
articles.summary: England striker Ivan Toney pleads not guilty to assaulting a man at a Soho nightclub last year.
articles.body:
England striker Ivan Toney has pleaded not guilty to assaulting a man at a central London nightclub.

The 30-year-old footballer, from Northampton, is accused of headbutting and punching Saber Da Silva at a nightclub in Wardour Street, Soho, on 6 December.

At Westminster Magistrates' Court, Toney confirmed his name and age, and pleaded not guilty to a charge of assault occasioning actual bodily harm.

District Judge Briony Clarke said the case could be tried in the magistrates court, but Toney elected for a Crown Court trial in front of a judge and jury.

He was freed on unconditional bail until a hearing at Southwark Crown Court on 29 October.

Toney won 10 caps for England and was part of the squad that reached the Euro 2024 final.

He started his football career with Northampton Town and played for teams including Wigan Athletic and Peterborough United before signing for Brentford in 2020.

He currently plays for Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli.

articles.title: Flydubai cockpit horror: Terror plot, suicide bid or Iran link? 5 chilling questions facing investigators
articles.summary: More than 24 hours after an attack aboard Flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, key questions remain unanswered about the incident that shook
articles.body: More than 24 hours after an attack aboard Flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, key questions remain unanswered about the incident that shook Israel and drew global attention.The aircraft was diverted to Saudi Arabia after the Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain in the cockpit and eventually landed safely in Tabuk. Investigators are now trying to establish the motive behind the attack, the identity and background of the alleged attacker, whether Iran had any role and how the incident was allowed to unfold aboard the flight.The flight departed Dubai at 6.05 am local time and was flying west towards Tel Aviv. About two hours after takeoff, it began losing altitude rapidly and turned sharply north, according to flight-tracking data. The aircraft descended 17,400 feet in just under two minutes before issuing a distress call at 8.31 am (local time).It then squawked code 7500, the International Civil Aviation Organization code used to indicate a hijacking, as passengers described chaotic scenes on board.Terror attack or suicide attempt?The motive behind the attack remains unclear, with questions over whether the alleged attacker intended to carry out a terror attack or was attempting suicide. US President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu discussed the incident “at length” over the phone. Trump said the co-pilot “was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job.”The UAE prosecutor general has ordered an investigation into the circumstances and motives behind the incident, including whether it was linked to militant activity or involved prior planning or direction. The Israeli Foreign Ministry described the incident to diplomats as an attempted terrorist attack aimed at undermining ties between Israel and the UAE.Who was the attacker?The attacker was identified as an Omani national serving as the co-pilot of the Flydubai flight. His identity and background remained unclear as investigators worked to establish what happened. The UAE prosecutor general has ordered an investigation into the incident.UAE judicial authorities have jurisdiction because the aircraft is registered in the UAE and operates under its flag. The UAE said its law applies to crimes committed on board “even if they occur outside the country's territory”. Netanyahu said he spoke with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who agreed Israel would participate in the interrogation of the suspect.The attacker was being investigated in Saudi Arabia, with Netanyahu saying he believed the suspect would later be taken to the UAE.Was Iran involved in the attack?Whether Iran had any role in the incident also remained unanswered. Netanyahu said Wednesday that it was too early to determine whether Iran was involved.“Well, it’s too early to say,” Netanyahu told Fox News when asked whether there was any indication of Iranian involvement. “The attacking pilot is now being investigated in Saudi Arabia,” Netanyahu said, adding he believed the suspect would be taken to UAE and Israel could participate.“It’s no secret that Iran wants to target Israelis abroad, wants to target Israel here,” Netanyahu said. He said Israel had also seen signs from Iran’s proxies of plans to attack, citing Hamas and Hezbollah ahead of Israel’s elections.“We have clear evidence of that,” Netanyahu said. “But I think that whether or not this was carried out as part of that plan, that we don’t know yet.”How was the weapon allowed on the plane?The incident has raised questions about how a knife could be brought into the cockpit by a member of the flight crew and whether existing security procedures are sufficient when the threat comes from within the crew. In the US, pilots and flight attendants undergo criminal history record checks, security threat assessments and identity verification.Netanyahu also said the captain was attacked by the co-pilot with an “axe”, adding that Smit “managed to unlock the door” even while wounded.Crew members use designated access points and can bypass passenger screening, although they may be randomly selected for physical screening by the Transportation Security Administration. Random screening can help prevent weapons from being carried by crew members but cannot eliminate every possibility of a determined crew member bringing a weapon into a secure area.US flight and cabin crew are also required to undergo recurrent security training, including self-defence and hijacking exercises. Security procedures for flight crews were strengthened after the September 11 attacks, with greater emphasis on resisting hijackings and protecting the flight deck.Why was the flight allowed to take off?Another question is how the attacker, described as an Omani national and religious extremist, was cleared to operate a flight to Israel. Israel is investigating how he was cleared to fly the Dubai-Tel Aviv route.The Israeli Foreign Ministry told diplomats that the incident was an attack aimed at undermining ties between Israel and the UAE and the Abraham Accords. Foreign Ministry Director General Eden Bar Tal briefed “all Israeli ambassadors and heads of representations around the world [during which] the message was emphasized that this was an attempted terrorist attack against Israelis, the United Arab Emirates and the Abraham Accords,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry referred to the Abraham Accords as the US-brokered normalization deal signed in 2020.Commercial pilots undergo a range of checks before flying, including medical certification. Assessments can include mental health screening, although requirements vary by country. In Australia, pilots undergo a background check to obtain an Aviation Security Identification Card. Background-check requirements vary between countries and may be limited to criminal history.If a person has no criminal record or documented warning, there may be nothing in the available checks to identify them as a security threat or risk.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Gujarat government on Thursday announced that they will award Indian pilot Smit Machchhar with the 'Visisht Gujarat Garima Award' for
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Gujarat government on Thursday announced that they will award Indian pilot Smit Machchhar with the 'Visisht Gujarat Garima Award' for fighting his copilot who allegedly planned to crash the flydubai plane that was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv.Captain Smit Machchhar was stabbed by his Omani co-pilot while fighting him in the cockpit, but fought back and was severely injured. The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia with all the passengers safe."The courage of Captain Smit Machchhar, the pilot of the flight headed to Israel, is being saluted by the entire world today. Despite being drenched in blood due to the attack, he displayed indomitable bravery to save the lives of 174 passengers—a feat that is profoundly inspiring and commendable," said Gujarat CM Bhupendra Patel on X.READ ALSO: Was Flydubai cockpit attack planned? UAE probe to examine possible terror link"This valiant son of Gujarat has illuminated the name of Gujarat and the nation across the globe through his heroism. The Gujarati spirit flowing in his veins fills us all with immense pride. To honor his extraordinary act of bravery and humanity, the Government of Gujarat will bestow upon Captain Smit Machhar the 'Visisht Gujarat Garima Award'," he added.Further praying for his swift recovery, the CM said, "The empathy and prayers of the nation's citizens are with Captain Smit Machchhar."Captain Smit Machchhar has been hailed for his courage after being stabbed by his Omani co-pilot during the Dubai-Tel Aviv flight, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump among those praising his actions. PM Modi said Machchhar had shown “remarkable patience, presence of mind, and courage” and described him as a “HERO”, saying his valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a major tragedy.Netanyahu also saluted Machchhar for his “extraordinary bravery”, saying that despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, opened the cockpit door and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker. Trump similarly called the Indian pilot “a hero”, saying that even while badly wounded, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door and call for help.Read more: PM Modi heaps praise on flydubai pilot Captain MachchharCaptain Smit Machchhar, a Mumbaikar from Ghatkopar, is a commercial pilot who trained in New Zealand for his commercial pilot licence and later completed his Boeing 737 type rating at FSTC in Manesar, Gurgaon. He worked with SpiceJet for about a decade before joining flydubai in 2022.Machchhar, who is in his mid-30s, comes from a family with aviation ties, with his brother also working as a flydubai pilot. Friends and former colleagues describe him as a calm, decent and hardworking professional who was always willing to learn. He is currently recovering after being injured in the cockpit attack.Read more: How Indian pilot Smit Machchhar stopped Omani co-pilot from crashing planeGet the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Fighter jets in air’: How Israel prepared for worst-case scenario during flydubai scare
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Israel scrambled fighter jets after a Dubai-Tel Aviv-bound flydubai aircraft transmitted emergency signals amid an alleged attempt by its
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Israel scrambled fighter jets after a Dubai-Tel Aviv-bound flydubai aircraft transmitted emergency signals amid an alleged attempt by its co-pilot to crash the plane, but the warplanes did not have to take action as passengers and crew managed to regain control and land safely in Saudi Arabia, Israeli envoy to India Reuven Azar said on Thursday.Speaking to PTI Videos in New Delhi, Azar said Israel's civil aviation authorities, air force and political leadership were immediately alerted after the aircraft reported an emergency. He said the situation was assessed as a potential threat given Israel's small geographical size and the possibility of an aircraft reaching its territory within seconds."Of course, immediately fighter jets were called into the air and fortunately, they didn't have to take action," Azar said.The envoy indicated that the situation could have escalated into a decision involving Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had the passengers and crew failed to regain control of the aircraft."They had assessed the situation, and if the pilot and the crew members and the passengers wouldn't have taken control of the plane, there could have been a situation in which the Prime Minister of Israel may have had to make a decision on the action to be taken," he said, without elaborating.READ ALSO: Was Flydubai cockpit attack planned? UAE probe to examine possible terror linkThe incident involved flydubai flight FZ1073, which was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv with 174 passengers, including 27 children. The aircraft reportedly made a sharp descent before diverting to Prince Sultan Bin Abdul Aziz Airport in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.Indian captain, Israeli passengers helped avert disasterAzar praised Indian captain Smit Machchhar for managing to open the cockpit door despite being attacked by his co-pilot, allowing passengers to intervene and prevent the aircraft from crashing.The envoy said three Israeli passengers onboard rushed towards the cockpit, subdued the alleged attacker and helped take preliminary control of the situation. They also called for a doctor to attend to the injured captain."In addition to that, there were two additional pilots on the flight... that few seconds after the Israelis entered the cabin... were able to take control of the flight and actually get it to fly safely and land in Saudi Arabia," Azar said.He said Machchhar had received appreciation from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, President Isaac Herzog, the speaker of the Parliament and people across Israel for his actions."So, we had here people, first of all, the Indian captain who has been really admired in Israel, both by the Prime Minister, the President, the head of the Parliament and the entire Israeli people for what he did. He saved so many lives," Azar said.The envoy added that the combined efforts of the Indian captain, Israeli passengers, crew members and additional pilots helped turn what could have been a catastrophic incident into a safe landing."we had a situation that from almost a secure crash of the plane, we had a secure landing and the saving of nearly 180 people," he said.Machchhar was injured during the alleged attack and was initially stabilised onboard by an Israeli doctor. Azar said Saudi authorities were subsequently providing him medical assistance after the aircraft landed in Tabuk.The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia had earlier identified Machchhar as an Indian national and said he was receiving treatment at a hospital in Tabuk in stable condition.READ ALSO: 'Indomitable bravery’: Indian Flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar to be awarded ‘Visisht Gujarat Garima Award’Investigation underway, motive remains unclearThe envoy said the investigation was still at a preliminary stage and authorities were yet to establish the motive behind the alleged attack."We are in a very preliminary stage. I think that following the investigation of the attacker, we'll be able to learn more," Azar said.The UAE's Attorney General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi has ordered an investigation into the incident to establish its circumstances, details and motives, including whether it was linked to any terrorist activity or involved prior planning.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has also said it was too early to determine whether Iran had any involvement in the incident. He indicated that Israel could participate in the investigation.The incident comes weeks ahead of Israel's October 27 legislative election and days before the country commemorates the October 7 Hamas-led attacks in 2023.Azar referred to the timing while discussing the incident but did not establish any connection between the alleged attack and the broader regional security situation."There's no doubt that the timing was very sensitive, you know. We are only a few weeks before an election in Israel. We are in a situation in which we are going to commemorate the 7th of October, the beginning of next week," he said.The flydubai spokesperson had also urged people to avoid speculation while authorities investigate the incident, saying the underlying reasons and motives remained unknown.You use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI: The UAE has ordered a probe into the Flydubai mid-air incident involving an alleged attempt by an Omani co-pilot to crash a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight, with investigators set to examine all circumstances and motives, including any possible links to terrorist activity, prior planning or direction.The UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA) said Attorney-General Counsellor Dr Hamad Al Shamsi had ordered the formation of a specialised Public Prosecution team to investigate the circumstances and causes of the incident involving Flydubai flight FZ1073.The flight, which departed from Dubai International Airport for Tel Aviv, was diverted and landed safely at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia after an altercation reportedly broke out in the cockpit. Flydubai had said its crew members travelling onboard intervened and secured the aircraft."The ministry noted that the investigation includes examining all circumstances and motives surrounding the incident, including any possible connection to terrorist activity or intent, and whether it involved prior planning or direction," the statement said.The ministry said UAE judicial authorities have jurisdiction to investigate the incident under applicable laws as the aircraft is registered in the UAE and operates under its flag. UAE law, it added, applies to crimes committed onboard the aircraft, including those occurring outside the country's territory.The UAE also thanked Saudi authorities for their cooperation and handling of the incident, while urging people to rely on official statements and avoid circulating speculation or unverified information until the investigation is completed.READ ALSO: 'Indomitable bravery’: Indian Flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar to be awarded ‘Visisht Gujarat Garima Award’Meanwhile, according to The Times of Israel, Saudi Arabia will conduct the initial investigation into the Omani pilot accused of attempting to crash the flight before handing him over to the UAE for further investigation.An Israeli official told the publication that Israel expects more significant findings to emerge from the Emirati investigation after the Saudi probe is completed.The incident involved Flydubai flight FZ1073, which was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv when it was diverted to Tabuk following an alleged attack on the Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, by his co-pilot.Machchhar was injured in the incident but managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to intervene. Three Israeli passengers reportedly helped subdue the attacker, while two additional pilots onboard took control of the aircraft and landed it safely in Saudi Arabia.You use AI every day. articles.title: Drumcree and Garvaghy Road policing operation has cost £3m
articles.summary: Chief Constable Jon Boutcher warns of the consequences and cost "if they get it wrong".
articles.body:
Chief Constable Jon Boutcher has said the policing operation over the Drumcree parading dispute has cost about £3m so far.

Speaking at a meeting of the Policing Board, he described the situation as "challenging" - but said that despite "very significant tensions" there had been no violence.

The stand-off - over a proposed Orange Orange parade in Portadown, opposed by nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road - has lasted since Sunday morning.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) has deployed a significant number of officers, with Boutcher saying he had a responsibility to preserve peace and maintain order.

He said the cost of the policing operation had been £3m thus far, but warned of the consequences and cost "if they get it wrong".

The consequences of police forcing an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road "could be catastrophic" for Northern Ireland, he added.

"I've made it clear to my senior team that our objective is to facilitate the Parades Commission determination," said Boutcher.

"The Parades Commission determination means that the Orange Order can lawfully parade down the Garvaghy Road. Without that determination, such a parade would be unlawful.

"What it does not mean, however, is that the police must accommodate that determination at all costs."

He said the police were not expected to "nor will they force" members of the Orange Order "through a hostile crowd".

Orange Order says no proposals on table to resolve Drumcree dispute

What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about?

During the meeting, it also emerged that the Policing Board has launched a code-of-conduct investigation into one of its members, Sinn Féin's Deirdre Hargey.

She was pictured taking part in an unlawful protest against the march on the Garvaghy Road on Sunday.

Hargey attended the board meeting after a failed attempt by Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) assembly member Trevor Clarke to have her barred.

With the PSNI currently being unable to police the Parades Commission ruling to allow the march , Boutcher said he was giving "space" for negotiations.

Under legislation, he can apply to the Northern Ireland secretary to have the determination overturned or amended.

Boutcher said: "The board needs to be reassured that I am constantly reviewing that position.

"But at this stage it is my judgement that that is not necessary.

"We are creating the time to resolve this and that is in the interests of everyone."

He said the investigation into the unlawful protest, which prevented the parade, was under way and was "fully resourced".

Boutcher said potential offences included unnotified protest, obstructing a lawful parade and breaching the Parades Commission determination.

"Believe me, the evidence gathering process has been extensive," he said.

"I want it to be thorough but I want it to be expeditious to send a clear message.

A fresh legal challenge by the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition is due to be heard in the courts on Friday.

Last Friday, the Parades Commission said the Orange Order's march could go ahead along Garvaghy Road.

Rather than start at 13:00 on Sunday as intended, the commission said it could begin no later than 08:00 and with 35 participants rather than the 60 the Orange Order requested.

But an initial legal challenge from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition (GRRC) at the High Court saw a judge issue an injunction banning the parade, with Judge Patricia Smyth saying the "long-running dispute has the potential to escalate within Northern Ireland".

This was later successfully challenged by an Orange Order member at the Court of Appeal.

Late on Saturday evening, the GRRC was given permission to challenge that decision at the High Court - an appeal which was dismissed by Justice Humphreys.

The Drumcree parade dispute began in the mid-1990s and almost derailed the peace process at the time.

Violence related to the dispute resulted in riots, roadblocks and murders.

When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995 there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.

The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches.

Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order - unsuccessfully - over the past three decades.

articles.title: Man admits posing as medical student at Aberdeen hospital
articles.summary: Stephen Simpson, 22, wore medical scrubs and NHS branded clothing at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.
articles.body:
A man has admitted pretending to be a medical student for several weeks and accessing Aberdeen hospital wards and files.

Stephen Simpson, 22, wore medical scrubs and NHS branded clothing at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary (ARI), as well as having a stethoscope.

At Aberdeen Sheriff Court, Simpson admitted fraud, between 9 December 2023 and 26 January 2024.

Sentence was deferred until later this month for reports. NHS Grampian has been asked for comment.

More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland

Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds

Simpson originally faced a total of six charges - one of fraud and five others of theft.

The fraud was alleged to have happened between 22 September 2023 and 26 January 2024.

However, solicitor Laura Gracie said Simpson was pleading guilty to two amended charges.

These were that Simpson, from Aberdeen, pretended to employees he was a medical student authorised to be in ARI.

Wearing medical scrubs and NHS branded clothing, and having a stethoscope and pager, he induced employees to allow him to remain in the hospital and gain access to restricted areas and files, staff-only areas, wards, and had access to medical files.

He also admitted stealing items of NHS branded clothing, a pager, and perfume.

The amended pleas were accepted by fiscal Dylan Middleton for the Crown.

Sheriff Morag McLaughlin deferred sentence for a criminal justice social work report and restriction of liberty order assessment.

articles.title: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
articles.summary: The president wants AI to be called super intelligence - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian domains.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official national registry.

The president wants AI to be called super intelligence - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian websites.

Register.si spokesperson Klara Herman said 44,000 web addresses with the .si suffix had been registered in September, compared to less than 2,000 in August - an increase of more than 2,100%.

She said the scale of activity in late September was "unprecedented" compared to the previous 12 months.

President Trump called for the technology to be renamed during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 11 September.

"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said.

"It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful... welcome to the new world of super intelligence."

Internet domains are the unique human-readable addresses people type into their web browsers to access websites - like bbc.co.uk.

Herman said registrations for .si web addresses in September stood out "very clearly" against the other months in the year, although she was "cautious" about attributing the entire increase to only President Trump's comments.

She said on 30 September alone, 11,000 new registrations were recorded.

One possible explanation for the purchases is cyber-squatting - where people speculatively register specific domain names in case they increase in value later on and can be sold for a profit.

For example, in 1997 Rick Schwartz, known as "The Domain King", bought the domain name men.com for $15,000 (£11,300). He sold it for $1.32 million seven years later.

On Tuesday, President Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the people "building America's Golden Age".

He signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and they should no longer acknowledge the use of the term AI.

SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.

Images of the signatures for the order were mocked online however - when it was discovered "United States" had been spelt incorrectly underneath President Trump's signature.
